name: Vantage

profile.reading:
This is one of three data center buildings on Vantage Data Centers' New Albany, Ohio campus at 3325 Horizon Court, in the New Albany International Business Park spanning Licking and Franklin counties, now one of the largest concentrations of hyperscale data center construction in the eastern United States. The park has drawn Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Vantage, attracted by AEP Ohio's transmission capacity, Ohio's data center sales and use tax exemption program, and local economic development incentive agreements negotiated with New Albany and Licking County.

Vantage's own campus materials describe the site as roughly 70 acres with about 1.5 million square feet planned across three two story buildings, each stated at approximately 64 megawatts of critical IT capacity, for a total campus capacity near 192 megawatts once fully built out. Vantage's page does not assign individual names, building numbers, or separately confirmed square footage figures to each of the three structures beyond this uniform per building description, so an even division of the 1.5 million total, approximately 500,000 square feet per building, is this profile's derived estimate rather than an operator confirmed figure for this specific building. Vantage has stated the first of the three buildings was slated to reach operational status in December 2025, with additional phases continuing through 2028. Power is supplied end to end at 480 volts, with N+1 electrical and N+2 mechanical redundancy per Vantage's standard design approach, and each building is targeted for LEED Silver certification.

Vantage's own company overview describes the New Albany project as an investment of more than 2 billion dollars and frames it as the company's entry into the Midwest United States market. Vantage Data Centers was founded in June 2010 with an investment from Silver Lake Partners and began by acquiring a former Intel data center in Santa Clara, California, before DigitalBridge became its majority owner in 2017. By its own current account the company operates more than 18 locations across North America, more than 15 across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and more than 9 across Asia Pacific. In 2024 its owners DigitalBridge and Silver Lake completed a 9.2 billion dollar equity investment in Vantage, later upsized by a further 2.8 billion dollars, to support global hyperscale customer demand, according to the company's own materials.

Ohio's rapid data center buildout, concentrated heavily in New Albany and neighboring Licking County communities, has become a subject of statewide debate over electricity rate impacts on residential ratepayers, prompting AEP Ohio to propose a distinct large load tariff classification for data centers before the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio.

reading:
This row, carrying the short name Vantage, is the same company as the Vantage Data Centers entry recorded elsewhere in this registry at uid 0213d483, a Denver headquartered wholesale developer backed by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake. The row is kept rather than deleted, per registry policy, and cross linked to the canonical entry, where the ownership history and full market list live. What this row usefully holds is a single campus, and that campus has a public record worth setting out on its own.

The three Ohio facilities here are buildings one, two and three of Vantage's New Albany campus at 3325 Horizon Court, in the Columbus metropolitan area. Vantage publishes 70 acres, three two storey buildings totalling about 1.5 million square feet, and 192 megawatts of critical IT load at 64 megawatts a building. That is stated as critical IT load rather than utility service, which is the more useful of the two numbers and the rarer one to find published. The first building was targeted to go operational in December 2025 with the remaining phases running through 2028. Vantage describes power from American Electric Power Ohio over multiple diverse feeds, N plus one electrical and N plus two mechanical redundancy, a closed loop chilled water system with air side economisers aimed at near zero water use effectiveness, LEED Silver for each building, four carrier points of entry and two meet me rooms per building.

The regulatory record around this campus is the more interesting half. Central Ohio is where the American data centre load problem became a rate case. In testimony before the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, AEP Ohio described data centre demand in central Ohio rising from about 100 megawatts in 2020 to around 600 megawatts in 2024, with projections near 5 gigawatts by 2030, and said it had received inquiries and preliminary service requests from more than 50 customers at over 90 sites totalling more than 30,000 megawatts. AEP had imposed a moratorium on new data centre service connections while the question was resolved. The commission ordered a data centre specific tariff and approved it in an order dated 9 July 2025. Customers above 25 megawatts must pay for at least 85 per cent of their subscribed monthly capacity, on contracts of up to twelve years with a four year ramp up, plus exit fees and financial assurance, with existing facilities grandfathered unless they expand past the 25 megawatt threshold. The order also required AEP to end the moratorium. The Ohio Manufacturers Association challenged the outcome, and the dispute went on to the Ohio Supreme Court.

New Albany itself publishes a data centre page, which is the sort of municipal document residents force into existence. The city says fifteen companies operate more than forty facilities there, that data centres are allowed only in its General Employment and Technology Manufacturing districts under standards above the base zoning code covering landscaping, architecture, screening and noise held to the average intensity of street traffic noise in the nearest residential district, and that new companies receive real property tax abatements typically running ten to fifteen years. On water, the city states that its data centres do not use large volumes daily and that it has not needed additional water capacity because of them. Vantage's closed loop design is consistent with that, though the city does not break its figures out by operator.
